opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a really interesting question, and I don't want to be snobbish about it. I try to judge the work on its merits rather than on where it appears. There's a lot of very thoughtful material on LessWrong and the Alignment Forum, some of it by people who've been thinking hard about these issues for a long time, often well before the mainstream academic community took them seriously. So I'd be wary of dismissing it just because it hasn't gone through the traditional channels.

That said, peer review does serve a purpose. When something appears in Nature, you know that, at least in principle, a few experts have scrutinised it, that the claims are reasonably well supported, and that it's situated in relation to the existing literature. On LessWrong, the quality varies enormously. You get some brilliant pieces alongside posts that are speculative, poorly grounded, or that reinvent ideas that philosophers or cognitive scientists explored decades ago without realising it. So the burden falls more on the reader to do the filtering.

There's also a matter of style and culture. A lot of LessWrong writing makes very confident claims about things like intelligence, agency, goals, and consciousness, and sometimes uses those words in ways that, from my perspective, carry a lot of philosophical baggage that isn't examined. Coming from a background that draws on Wittgenstein and on embodied cognition, I'm often wary of the anthropomorphic language. Saying a large language model "wants" something or "believes" something can slip in assumptions without anyone noticing.

On the other hand, peer review isn't perfect either. It's slow, it can be conservative, and in a field moving as quickly as AI, a lot of the most important conversations happen on arXiv, blogs, and forums long before anything reaches a journal. So in practice I read across all of these, and I bring the same critical attitude to each: what exactly is being claimed, what's the evidence, and are the concepts being used carefully? The venue gives you a prior, but it shouldn't be the last word.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that I try to judge the work on its merits rather than on where it appears, but that's easier said than done, and the two venues really do serve quite different functions.

Something that's gone through Nature has been through a process. Reviewers have looked at it, there's been some gatekeeping, the claims have had to be stated in a form that could survive scrutiny. That's not a guarantee of truth, of course, and we all know examples of things in prestigious journals that turned out to be wrong or overblown. But it means there's a kind of baseline you can rely on. With LessWrong there's no such filter. Anybody can post anything, and the quality is enormously variable. You'll find things that are genuinely insightful sitting alongside things that are, frankly, confused, and the voting system only partly sorts that out because it reflects the preferences of a particular community with a particular set of assumptions.

Having said that, I've found some LessWrong posts to be more intellectually stimulating than a great many peer-reviewed papers. The format allows for speculation, for thinking out loud, for raising questions that haven't yet been formulated precisely enough to go in a journal. And some of the discussion around AI alignment, around agency, around how we should conceptualise these systems, got going there years before it appeared in mainstream academic venues. So I'd be foolish to dismiss it.

Where I become more cautious is when ideas from that community get treated as established results rather than as interesting conjectures. There's a tendency, in some of that writing, towards a particular style of reasoning, long chains of plausible-sounding inferences, and the conclusions can end up being held with a confidence that the arguments don't really warrant. Philosophers are trained to be suspicious of that, and I think rightly so. The absence of an adversarial reader, someone whose job is to find the hole in your argument, does show.

So to put it bluntly, I'd read a LessWrong post the way I'd read a working paper or a blog post from a clever colleague. It might change how I think about something, but I'd want to see the idea tested, formalised, criticised, before I'd lean on it. Whereas with something in Nature, I start from a position of somewhat greater trust, while still reading critically, because peer review catches less than people imagine.

astra-6.text: Well, I would want to judge the work on its merits. Peer review gives you some degree of quality control, so publication in a journal like Nature carries weight, but it’s certainly not a guarantee that something is right. Equally, something being published on LessWrong isn’t a reason to dismiss it. You have to look at the argument, the evidence, and how it stands up to criticism. Of course, when it’s outside your own expertise, that’s much harder, and then the judgments of people with relevant expertise become important.

r001.rationale: The response says to judge the work on its merits and explains that neither Nature publication guarantees correctness nor LessWrong publication warrants dismissal.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I would want to judge the particular piece of work rather than simply where it appeared. Peer review gives you a certain amount of confidence that something has been scrutinised, but it certainly doesn't guarantee that it's right. And the absence of peer review doesn't mean that something isn't insightful.

With LessWrong, I'd look for clarity about the assumptions, the quality of the argument, and whether the author engages seriously with objections and relevant research. I'd ask those same questions of a paper in Nature. The venue is a useful signal, but it shouldn't substitute for examining the work itself.

r001.rationale: The response says to judge the particular work rather than where it appeared, and to apply the same substantive questions to both venues.
